mainEntity.name: Is a CD or a high-yield savings account better?

acceptedAnswer.text: A CD usually wins if you won't need the money before it matures and rates fall or stay flat. A high-yield savings account wins if you may need the money, or if rates rise during the term. Many savers use both.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I withdraw from a CD early?

acceptedAnswer.text: You pay an early withdrawal penalty, commonly a set number of days or months of interest. If you break the CD early enough, the penalty can exceed the interest earned and reduce your principal.

mainEntity.name: Do high-yield savings account rates change?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. HYSA rates are variable and banks can change them at any time, typically following moves in the Federal Reserve's policy rate.

mainEntity.name: Are CDs and high-yield savings accounts insured?

acceptedAnswer.text: At FDIC-insured banks, both are covered up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Credit union accounts have equivalent NCUA coverage.

mainEntity.name: Which earns more, a CD or a high-yield savings account?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the rates and on how the savings rate changes. If the HYSA rate holds, a CD pays more only if its APY is higher. If HYSA rates fall, the CD earns more. On $10,000 for 24 months, a 4.50% CD earns $920.25 against $716.48 for a HYSA that starts at 4.00% and falls 0.5 point a year.

mainEntity.name: When does a high-yield savings account beat a CD?

acceptedAnswer.text: When its rate is higher than the CD's for most of the term, or rises during it, or when you need access to the money. A HYSA also wins if breaking the CD would cost more in penalty than the CD earns over the savings account.

mainEntity.name: Is a CD safer than a high-yield savings account?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both are insured the same way, up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, at an FDIC-insured bank or NCUA-insured credit union. The difference is rate risk and access, not safety of principal.

mainEntity.name: Should I keep my emergency fund in a CD?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually no. An emergency fund needs instant access, and a CD charges a penalty for early withdrawal. A HYSA is the usual choice, with any extra cash in CDs.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a money market account and a money market fund?

acceptedAnswer.text: A money market account is a bank deposit account that is insured up to the limit. A money market fund is an investment product, is not FDIC insured, and can in rare cases lose value.

mainEntity.name: Can I have a CD and a HYSA at the same time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many savers keep emergency cash in a HYSA and the rest in CDs, often laddered so that one matures every year.

mainEntity.name: Is a high-yield savings rate fixed?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. HYSA rates are variable, and banks can change them at any time, usually after the Federal Reserve changes its policy rate.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth opening a HYSA for a small balance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often yes, if the account has no monthly fee and a low or no minimum balance. The difference in rate still applies: $1,000 at 4.00% earns $40 a year, against $4 at 0.40%.
